claim: India's nutraceutical market reached USD 30.37 billion in 2024 and the global nutraceutical market was valued at USD 591.1 billion in 2024, projected to grow at 7.6% CAGR through 2030.
stance_target: Size and growth of nutraceutical market relevant to Briyo's business context
quoted_support: With the global market valued at USD 591.1 billion in 2024 and projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.6% (2025–2030)... India is emerging as a key player, with its nutraceutical market reaching USD 30.37 billion in 2024, fueled by rising FDI, a booming middle class, and increasing consumer preference for immunity-boosting and wellness products.

claim: India's nutraceuticals are regulated as foods under FSSAI's FSS Act 2006 and FSS (Nutra) Regulation 2022, with no pre-market clinical trial requirement — far less stringent than pharmaceutical regulation.
stance_target: Indian nutraceutical regulatory framework is inadequate to ensure quality and safety of products like Briyo D3
quoted_support: In India, even though it is sold in the form of medicines, nutraceutical products are categorized as foods and regulated accordingly. They are regulated under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act), and the manufacturing and marketing of these products are monitored by the FSS Authority of India (FSSAI). They are not strictly regulated as that of pharmaceuticals.

claim: The Indian government formed a panel in 2024 to consider shifting nutraceutical regulation from FSSAI to CDSCO (the pharmaceutical drug regulator), signaling regulatory tightening ahead.
stance_target: Future regulatory risk for supplement brands in India including Briyo
quoted_support: Recently, the Union Government has formed a panel to analyze the possibility of shifting the regulation of nutraceutical products to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization, the main drug regulatory body in India. The officials also highlighted that because of unclear demarcation, many companies are opting to seek approval from FSSAI for products having therapeutic properties that closely resemble pharmaceutical products.

claim: The Delhi High Court ruled that nutraceuticals should be treated on par with pharmaceuticals and subject to the same stringent passing-off tests (Sun Pharma v. Ajanta Pharma, 2019).
stance_target: Legal precedent suggesting Indian nutraceutical brands face pharmaceutical-level accountability
quoted_support: The Delhi High Court in Sun Pharma Laboratories Ltd. v Ajanta Pharma Ltd. observed that the mere fact that the products are nutraceuticals and not pharmaceuticals in the strict sense, and contain only plant-derived ingredients, is not convincing enough for less stringent tests for passing off. They are similar to pharmaceutical products, and both are used for the improvement of the health of patients.

claim: Nutraceuticals in India can be sold in tablet/capsule/softgel form and must comply with Indian Pharmacopoeia purity and quality standards when FSSAI hasn't specified requirements.
stance_target: Quality standards applicable to Briyo Vitamin D3 softgels
quoted_support: The existing regulations also specified that these products can be delivered in the form of capsules, tablets, granules, powders, drops, etc. When nutraceutical products are delivered in the form of tablets, capsules, granules, etc., the purity criteria and quality requirements must comply with the requirements specified in the Indian Pharmacopoeia, if the Food Authority does not specify the requirements.
